```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)

library(dplyr)
library(tidyverse)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)

library(p8105.datasets)
data("ny_noaa")
```

***PROBLEM 1***
```{r, warning = FALSE}
# Exploring the data
head(ny_noaa)
ncol(ny_noaa)
nrow(ny_noaa)

# Quantifying missing data
sum(is.na(ny_noaa))
colSums(is.na(ny_noaa))
```
This dataset includes information about NOAA stations in New York, including date, precipitation and snowfall levels, and maximum and minimum temperature. This dataset includes 7 variables and 2,595,176 observations, though a significant portion of observations are missing, most significantly for maximum and minimum temperature variables. This may be a problem when trying to draw conclusions about, for example, monthly minimum and maximum temperatures, if a certain month was particularly afflicted by missing values. 

```{r, warning = FALSE}
# Separating date into month, day, year
ny_noaa_clean <- ny_noaa %>%
  separate(date,
           into = c("year", "month", "day"),
           sep = "-")

# Converting variable types and units
ny_noaa_clean <- ny_noaa_clean %>%
  mutate(
    across(c(year, month, day, prcp, snow, snwd, tmax, tmin),
           as.numeric),
    prcp = prcp / 10,
    tmax = tmax / 10,
    tmin = tmin / 10
  )

head(ny_noaa_clean)

# Most commonly observed values for snowfall
common_snow_noaa <- ny_noaa_clean %>%
  count(snow, sort = TRUE) %>%
  slice_head(n = 10)

common_snow_noaa
```
I cleaned the data by separating the date column into separate year, month, and day variables using the separate() function. I also converted all variables to numeric using the mutate() function. The most commonly observed values for snowfall in millimeters were 0 and NA. This makes sense because during most days of the year, it does not snow at all, and this dataset is missing many observations.

```{r, warning = FALSE}
# Filtering and calculating tmax means for January and July
janjuly_tmax <- ny_noaa_clean %>%
  filter(month %in% c(1, 7)) %>%
  group_by(id, year, month) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

head(janjuly_tmax)

# Removing NaN values before plotting
janjuly_tmax_no_nan <- janjuly_tmax %>%
  filter(!is.nan(mean_tmax))

# Plot: Tmax Jan & July across years, by station
janjuly_tmax_plot <- ggplot(
  janjuly_tmax_no_nan,
  aes(
    x = year,
    y = mean_tmax,
    color = id,
    group = id
  )
) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.4, linewidth = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~month, scales = "fixed",
    labeller = labeller(
      month = c("1" = "January", "7" = "July")
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Maximum Temperature by Station Across Years",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Average Maximum Temperature (°C)",
    color = "Station"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    panel.spacing = unit(1, "cm")
  )

janjuly_tmax_plot
```
The average maximum temperature was significantly higher in July than in January across weather stations, as expected due to seasonal differences. There was quite a bit of variation in average maximum temperature readings between stations, but the overall temperature patterns of the stations were still relatively similar. There seems to be an undulating pattern of warmer and cooler maximum temperatures every few years. A few stations had unusually high or low average temperatures in certain years, such as the unusually cool July datapoint around 1988, which may represent outliers.

```{r, warning = FALSE}
# Plot: Tmax and Tmin for full dataset
tmax_tmin_full <- ggplot(
  ny_noaa_clean,
  aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)
) +
  geom_bin2d() +
  labs(
    title = "Maximum vs. Minimum Temperature",
    x = "Minimum Temperature (°C)",
    y = "Maximum Temperature (°C)",
    fill = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# Plot: Distribution of snowfall 0-100 by year
snow_distribution_plot <- ny_noaa_clean %>%
  filter(snow > 0, snow < 100) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(year), y = snow)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  labs(
    title = "Snowfall Distribution by Year",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Snowfall (mm)"
  ) +
  scale_x_discrete(
  breaks = as.character(seq(1981, 2010, by = 5))
) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(
      angle = 90,
      hjust = 1
    )
  )

# Combining into a two-panel plot
tmax_tmin_snow_plot <- tmax_tmin_full + snow_distribution_plot

tmax_tmin_snow_plot
```

***PROBLEM 2***
```{r, warning = FALSE}
# Exploring the data
accel_demo_raw <- read.csv("data/nhanes_covar.csv", skip = 4)
head(accel_demo_raw)

accel_data_raw <- read.csv("data/nhanes_accel.csv")
head(accel_data_raw)

# Merging datasets by SEQN
accel_data_clean <- merge(accel_demo_raw, accel_data_raw, by = "SEQN")

# Cleaning variable names
accel_data_clean <- janitor::clean_names(accel_data_clean)

# Converting variable types
accel_data_clean <- mutate(
  accel_data_clean,
  education = as.factor(education),
  sex = as.character(sex),
  sex = case_match(
    sex,
    "1" ~ "male",
    "2" ~ "female",
    .default = "NA"
  ),
  sex = as.factor(sex)
)

# Filtering out participants under 21 or with missing demographic data
accel_data_clean <- accel_data_clean %>%
  drop_na(sex, age, bmi, education) %>%
  filter(age >= 21)
head(accel_data_clean)

# Creating a table of men and women by education level
accel_data_ed_names <- mutate(
  accel_data_clean,
  education = as.character(education),
  education = case_match(
    education,
    "1" ~ "Less than high school",
    "2" ~ "High school",
    "3" ~ "More than high school",
      .default = "NA"
    )
  )

accel_education_table <- accel_data_ed_names %>%
  count(education, sex) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = sex,
    values_from = n
  )

accel_education_table <- knitr::kable(
  accel_education_table,
  col.names = c("Education Category", "Men", "Women"),
  caption = "Number of Men and Women by Education Category"
)
accel_education_table

# Plot: Age distribution of men and women in each education category
age_dist_ed_plot <- ggplot(
  accel_data_ed_table,
  aes(x = sex, y = age, fill = sex)
) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_wrap(~ education) +
  labs(
    title = "Age Distribution by Sex and Education Level",
    x = "Sex",
    y = "Age (years)",
    fill = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
age_dist_ed_plot
```
Looking at the table, it appears that there is not a large difference between the number of males and females in the groups with less than or more than a high school education, whereas females make up a noticeably higher proportion of the high school education group. Additionally, those with more than a high school education made up the largest group across both sexes.

Looking at the plot, participants with more than a high school education appear to trend younger than the other two education groups, with the median age being relatively similar between males and females. The median age between the sexes in the group with less than a high school education is also relatively similar, whereas in the high school education group, the age of males appears to trend younger than females.

```{r, warning = FALSE}
# Aggregating total activity
accel_total_act <- accel_data_ed_names %>%
  mutate(
    total_activity = rowSums(
      across(starts_with("min")),
      na.rm = TRUE
    )
  )

# Plot: Total activity by age, education level and sex
accel_total_act_plot <- ggplot(
  accel_total_act,
  aes(x = age, y = total_activity, color = sex)
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ education) +
  labs(
    title = "Total Daily Activity by Age, Sex, and Education",
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Total Activity",
    color = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
accel_total_act_plot
```
Looking at the plot, it appears that total daily activity generally decreases with age across all education categories, although the trends vary between males and females. In the high school education group, activity levels appear to decline after around age 40 for both sexes. In the less than high school education group, activity also generally decreases with age, with some fluctuations in the trend lines. In the more than high school education group, activity levels are more variable, but both males and females show a general decline at older ages. There are some differences between males and females, but neither sex consistently has higher activity across age groups or education categories. Overall, the plot shows substantial individual variation in activity levels.

```{r, warning = FALSE}
# Reshaping data 
accel_data_long <- accel_data_ed_names %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("min"),
    names_to = "minute",
    values_to = "activity"
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    minute = as.numeric(str_remove(minute, "min")),
    hour = minute / 60
  )

# Plot: 24hr activity time course by education and sex
accel_time_course_plot <- ggplot(
  accel_data_long,
  aes(x = hour, y = activity, color = sex)
) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ education, nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Daily Activity Courses by Education and Sex",
    x = "Time of Day (Hours)",
    y = "Average Activity",
    color = "Sex"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(0, 24, by = 4),
    limits = c(0, 24)
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

accel_time_course_plot
```
Looking at the plot, it appears that there are relatively similar daily activity patterns across all three education levels. For both males and females, activity is lowest around 4 AM, and increases quickly beginning around 6–8 AM. Activity stays relatively high throughout the day, then declines during the evening, particularly between 8PM-12AM. In the groups with less than high school and more than high school education, females generally show higher average activity than men during the day. In the high school education group, the differences between males and females are smaller, but female activity is somewhat higher during the middle of the day.
